summary.text: An electron shell is like an orbit that electrons follow around an atom's nucleus, and the closest one is called the K shell.
Each shell holds a fixed number of electrons: up to two in the first, eight in the second and 18 in the third.
Each period of the periodic table represents an electron shell, an idea that comes from Sommerfeld's modification of Bohr's 1913 model.

facts.label: Closest shell
facts.value: Called the 1 shell, or K shell

facts.label: Capacity rule
facts.value: The nth shell holds up to 2(n²) electrons

facts.label: Spin added
facts.value: Wolfgang Pauli added a fourth quantum number, spin, in 1925

facts.label: Shell letters
facts.value: K, L, M, N, O, P and Q

items.prompt: An atom's second shell is completely full. How many electrons does it hold?
items.explain: The first shell holds up to two electrons, the second up to eight and the third up to 18.

items.prompt: A teacher points to one row of the periodic table and says it stands for something about every atom in it. What does it stand for?

options.label: The number of neutrons each atom carries
The year each element was first isolated
The temperature at which each element melts
One electron shell of the atoms

items.explain: Each period on the conventional periodic table represents an electron shell.

items.prompt: Moseley measured X-rays from elements between calcium and zinc and saw the frequencies rise as the elements got heavier. What did this suggest was happening inside the atoms?

options.label: Electrons were emitting X-rays when they shifted to lower shells
Protons were being shed from the nucleus one by one
The nucleus was spinning faster in each heavier element
Electrons were leaving the atom whenever X-rays arrived

items.explain: The rising frequencies led to the theory that electrons emit X-rays when they shift to lower shells, which pointed to shells with a definite limit of electrons.

items.prompt: Barkla began his lettering at K, and later experiments showed that the K absorption lines come from a particular group of electrons. Which group?

options.label: Those that sit farthest out in the atom
Those closest to the nucleus
Those that spin fastest of all
Those shared between neighbouring atoms

items.explain: Later experiments showed that the K absorption lines are produced by the innermost electrons, matching the K shell closest to the nucleus.

items.prompt: A student pictures a shell as one solid ring with a single spot for electrons. What is actually inside a shell?

options.label: Only a single orbital shared by every electron in the shell
A set of identical rings, one for each electron in the shell
One or more subshells, each made of one or more atomic orbitals
A smooth cloud with no smaller parts of any kind

items.explain: Each shell consists of one or more subshells, and each subshell consists of one or more atomic orbitals.

items.prompt: Bohr's model used circular orbits. Sommerfeld kept the planetary picture but changed the orbits to better explain fine detail in some elements' spectra. What did he change?

options.label: He made the orbits mildly elliptical
He made the orbits perfectly square
He removed the orbits and used straight lines
He made every orbit the same size

items.explain: Sommerfeld retained Bohr's planetary model but added mildly elliptical orbits to explain the fine spectroscopic structure of some elements.

paragraphs.heading: What a shell is
paragraphs.text: An electron shell can be pictured as a path that electrons travel around the nucleus of an atom. The shell nearest the nucleus is the 1 shell, also called the K shell; next comes the 2 or L shell, then the 3 or M shell, each one farther out. The numbers are the principal quantum numbers, n = 1, 2, 3 and so on, and the letters come from X-ray notation.

paragraphs.heading: How many electrons fit
paragraphs.text: Each shell has room for only a fixed number of electrons. The first holds up to two, the second up to eight and the third up to 18; in general the nth shell can hold up to 2(n²). Each shell is built from one or more subshells, and each subshell from one or more atomic orbitals. On the usual periodic table, every period stands for one electron shell.

paragraphs.heading: Subshell labels
paragraphs.text: Subshells carry a lowercase letter for their type. The 4s subshell, for example, is an s-type subshell in the fourth, or N, shell. Each type has its own azimuthal quantum number, ℓ, a number whose exact meaning comes from quantum mechanics. An s-type subshell, such as 1s or 2s, can hold at most two electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word came from
paragraphs.text: The term shell comes from Arnold Sommerfeld's change to Bohr's 1913 model. Bohr was then working with Walther Kossel, whose papers of 1914 and 1916 called the orbits shells. Sommerfeld kept Bohr's planet-like picture but added mildly elliptical orbits to explain fine detail in the spectra of some elements. Electrons with the same n had orbits close together, forming a shell with real thickness rather than Bohr's flat circular rings.

paragraphs.heading: Evidence from X-rays
paragraphs.text: Shells were first seen in experiments by Charles Barkla and Henry Moseley, who studied how elements absorb X-rays. Moseley measured the X-ray frequencies of every element from calcium to zinc and found they rose as the elements got heavier. That led to the idea that electrons give off X-rays when they shift to lower shells, and that each shell has a set limit, with shells labelled K, L, M, N, O, P and Q. Barkla had started his labels at K in 1911 in case there were lines before his earlier 'A', and later work showed the K lines come from the innermost electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Chemists and the final rule
paragraphs.text: From 1913 to 1925 many chemists and a few physicists worked on placing electrons in shells. Chemists such as Irving Langmuir, Charles Bury and Gilbert Lewis put a limit of two in the first shell and eight in the next, and used the outer shells to explain valency. Bohr outlined his own shell theory in 1922, and it was basically the same as Bury's 1921 paper. In 1923 Edmund Stoner introduced the 2(n²) rule that is still used today, and two years later Wolfgang Pauli brought in spin as a fourth quantum number to complete the modern theory.
